newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobuto rejects pressure to deal with Zaire rebels.
newsitem.headline: Mobuto rejects pressure to deal with Zaire rebels.

text.p: Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko remains unmoved by mounting domestic pressure for a deal with rebels who are increasing their territorial conquests in eastern Zaire, a close political associate said on Sunday.
In a related development, Zaire denied U.N. charges of arming hardline Rwandan Hutus among about 200,000 refugees trapped in a forest camp near the city of Kisangani.
A threat by rebel leader Laurent Kabila that his guerrillas could attack the Tingi-Tingi camp in three days has prompted renewed calls for dialogue even from Mobutu's political allies.

"The position of the president is the same as that of the government. There can be no talks with a rebel who has taken up arms to destabilise the country," said Mobutu associate Banza Mukalay who met Mobutu at his remote Gbadolite palace on Friday.

Banza, who is Mobutu's deputy in the president's Popular Movement party, said Kabila was not interested in Zaire's faltering moves towards democracy. The country's first truly democratic elections were planned for next May before Tutsi-led rebels took up arms in eastern Zaire last October.
"I am astonished that political parties pressing for democracy are in favour of negotiations with the puppet (Kabila)," Banza told Reuters.
The central government in Kinshasa accuses Kabila of waging a proxy war for neighbouring Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi. All three deny Zaire's charges that their troops are involved.

Ethnic Tutsis launched the war accusing the Zairean authorities of denying them citizenship and of plans to expel them to Rwanda, their ancestral home. They now hold towns and territory along the border with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda.

Rebel thrusts on several fronts have blunted a mercenary-backed counter-offensive the army launched on January 20. The military says it is reinforcing Zaire's third city of Kisangani and Buta to the north and Kindu to the south.
U.N. and Tanzanian officials said up to 1,500 civilians were crossing Lake Tanganyika daily to escape advances in eastern Zaire, joined by smaller numbers of ragged Zairean soldiers.
They said on Sunday there were already more than 15,000 Zairean refugees in camps around Kigoma on the eastern shore of the lake in Tanzania.
Kabila has given Mobutu, who spent half of last year in France recovering from prostate surgery, until February 21 to begin talks on stepping down.
Another Mobutu ally, business tycoon and parliamentarian Bemba Saolona, on Sunday renewed his support for calls by Zaire's radical opposition for a negotiated settlement.
"The rebels continue their advance. The military option will lead nowhere. There is no telling how long the war will last if there is no negotiation," Bemba told Reuters.
Noting that 1997 was supposed to be an election year, he added: "We ought to negotiate with the rebels so that after the war elections can be held over the entire territory of Zaire."
U.N. special envoy Mohammed Sahnoun met Mobutu in Gbadolite on Saturday and returned to Kinshasa for more talks to try and avert an attack on Tingi Tingi as threatened by Kabila.
U.N. officials in New York said Sahnoun was carrying a message of concern to the Kinshasa government from U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan about the plight of refugees.

Both Annan and the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata have cautioned that civilians clustered round Tingi Tingi 205 km (120 miles) south of Kisangani, could be the main victims if Hutu hardliners make a stand there against rebels.
But in a statement on Sunday, the defence ministry said it "denies firmly allegations that Zaire is arming the ex-FAR (exiled ex-Rwandan soldiers) in the Tingi Tingi refugee camp.
It reaffirmed the Zaire army's resolve to puruse its counter-offensive.
